title: POC Weekly Caching Sync - NovaPay
summary: Weekly POC sync to review caching pilot results. Discussed prefix and KV cache hit rates improvements after prompt normalization, issues with low hit rate on certain user flows, suggestions for deterministic prompt keys, TTL policies, and monitoring. Agreed next steps: run per-endpoint hit-rate heatmap, instrument end-to-end trace for low-hit examples, apply prompt canonicalization for checkout flow, and follow up with security on KMS implications for cached payloads.
next_steps: Redwood to share updated caching config and expected hit-rate uplift projection (Jordan) by 2026-11-20
NovaPay to provide 24 sample low-hit conversations and associated request/response pairs (Marcus) by 2026-11-19
Priya to add per-endpoint cache heatmap to dashboard and enable 1h TTL experiment (Priya) by 2026-11-22
Schedule security sync about KMS/cache encryption (Jordan + Liam) week of 2026-11-23
action_items: Jordan: send caching config (include prefix rules, key derivation) - due 2026-11-20
Marcus: export 24 examples of low KV-hit interactions and upload to shared drive - due 2026-11-19
Priya: enable hit-rate heatmap, add alert for <30% hit-rate on high QPS endpoints - due 2026-11-22
Liam: confirm KMS policy requirements for caching sensitive fields - due 2026-11-24
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-11-17
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Marcus Chen (NovaPay Head of ML), Sofia Alvarez (NovaPay Platform), Liam O'Connor (NovaPay Security), Avery (Product), Tom - Eng

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining the weekly caching sync. quick roll call?
[00:08] Marcus: Marcus here.
[00:09] Sofia: Sofia.
[00:10] Liam: Liam on.
[00:11] Priya: Priya here.
[00:12] Jordan: Great. We'll start with the hit-rate numbers we promised. Priya, want to kick off?
[00:20] Priya: Yep. So this week we ran the normalization patch and adjusted the prefix canonicalization for the checkout and support flows. Overall KV cache hit-rate went from ~18% to 46% on aggregate across the pilot endpoints. Prefix-only cache (i.e., prefix match for common opens) improved from 28% to 55% on the support flow specifically.
[00:40] Marcus: Wait 46% aggregate, that's pretty good — are those numbers across all traffic or just sampled sessions?
[00:46] Priya: Sampled — we used a 10% production sample, plus full replay of the synthetic workload you shared. The aggregate combines embeddings re-routes and generation endpoints, so embedding requests dilute the number a bit. If you isolate generation-only it's closer to 52%.
[01:05] Sofia: For the checkout flow we still see low hits on new device sessions; it seems like session identifiers are leaking into the prompt somehow so the keys never match.
[01:15] Tom: yep that was our suspicion, different browser headers and some session tokens appended to the prompt template by a middleware.
[01:22] Priya: We flagged a few examples where the prompt had a device id or a timestamp. We recommended a prompt canonicalization step before keying — strip session-specific metadata and normalize spacing/case.
[01:35] Marcus: Can you show one of the low-hit examples?
[01:38] Priya: Sure, pulling one up. Example A: "checkout cart: items 3, user: XXXX-SESS-324..." In the canonicalized version that becomes "checkout cart items 3" which maps to the same prefix key as other sessions.
[01:55] Jordan: Quick comment, when you canonicalize, make sure you don't strip user-intent tokens that change the output, e.g., "apply discount code FOX10" vs "apply discount code none" — those change model behavior and shouldn't collide.
[02:10] Priya: Totally — our rule is to whitelist semantic tokens (discount codes, promo flags) and strip ephemeral metadata (session ids, timestamps, UA strings).
[02:20] Marcus: Another question — what TTL are you testing now? I remember we were conservative earlier.
[02:25] Priya: Right now we ran a 30m TTL baseline and an experimental 1h TTL for the high-traffic support flow. The 1h TTL gave a further 6-8% lift on hit-rate but raised some staleness concerns for user-specific config.
[02:39] Liam: From security standpoint, we need to ensure nothing PII-ish is stored in the cache unencrypted. If the prompt contains account numbers or partial PAN we need to either strip or encrypt and rotate keys.
[02:50] Jordan: We can do field-level redaction before caching and integrate with KMS for encryption at rest. Also Redwood supports per-tenant KMS keys for the cache store in the private deployment.
[03:04] Liam: Good. For the hosted pilot, we'll need to see the KMS flow and audit logs.
[03:10] Jordan: We'll add that to the security deep-dive next week.
[03:13] Priya: Back to metrics — we also instrumented prefix reuse across different user intents. For example, the helpdesk FAQ prompts have very high prefix reuse because the opening line is almost identical across users.
[03:25] Sofia: One oddity — the FAQ endpoint had a lot of cache evictions during the midday spike; are we hitting memory limits?
[03:32] Priya: Yes, we saw eviction thrashing on the edge cache tier. We adjusted the LRU window and increased memory allocation for that pool in the experiment which reduced evictions by ~40%.
[03:44] Marcus: Any impact on latency from the extra memory ops?
[03:48] Priya: Negligible; p99 latency stayed within the 300ms SLO for generation. Some p95 improvements actually.
[03:56] Jordan: Good to know. Marcus, you mentioned some low-hit conversations you uploaded last week — did you find patterns?
[04:03] Marcus: Yes, most of them were either UI-injected debug strings or user-auth tokens appended. A minority were genuine long-tail queries that don't share prefixes.
[04:13] Priya: For the UI debug strings we can add a regex-based sanitizer pre-keying. For the long-tail queries we recommend fallback caching (short TTL) or batching to amortize cost rather than trying to force reuse.
[04:26] Tom: On engineering side, what's the easiest place to add the canonicalization? Our stack currently adds metadata in the ingress layer.
[04:32] Priya: Ideal is to canonicalize right at the service boundary before Redwood's agent constructs the cache key, so it's consistent across clients. If you can add a microservice in the ingress chain that normalizes keys that's easiest.
[04:45] Tom: Ok we'll prototype that.
[04:47] Jordan: We should also discuss key derivation: whether to include model version, route, tenant id in the key. Priya?
[04:56] Priya: Our recommendation: key = hash(tenant_id | model_id | route | canonical_prompt_prefix). That avoids cross-tenant bleed and ensures model changes don't cold-start into wrong buckets. Also allows safe rollouts when you switch model weights.
[05:10] Marcus: What's the size of the key namespace? Are we likely to face hot-key issues?
[05:14] Priya: With prefixing we reduce cardinality but hotspots can emerge for very common prefixes. We recommend sharding keys with a small consistent hash salt (e.g., mod 64) for hot prefixes.
[05:26] Sofia: How does this interact with KV cache and prefix cache? Are we double-checking both?
[05:31] Priya: Yes, we have two layers: prefix cache that handles reuse of initial tokens (prefix-level), and KV cache which holds full sequence caches for autoregressive decoding. The key derivation is used for both; prefix cache keys are coarser.
[05:45] Marcus: Any telemetry we can add to identify hot prefixes automatically?
[05:49] Priya: We added a top-100 prefix heatmap that shows QPS by prefix hash and hit-rate. We'll be surfacing that to your dashboard today. That's one of the next steps.
[06:00] Jordan: Let's talk about the bench runs Redwood did on the 2 model variants we tested last week. Priya?
[06:06] Priya: Sure. We ran both the quantized 8-bit and the fp16 variants. With effective caching and prefetching the quantized variant had ~1.9x cost improvement with <3% change in accuracy on the eval prompt set. Latency increased slightly at p50 (~10ms) but p95 held.
[06:25] Marcus: The tiny accuracy delta is acceptable for support flows but not for high-risk decisioning in checkout.
[06:33] Jordan: Yes agreed — for checkout we recommend pinning fp16 or higher. Also we can set routing rules: checkout -> fp16, support -> quantized.
[06:42] Sofia: Is there an easy way to split traffic for canary? We want 10% on quantized for checkout to see if any real-world regressions.
[06:49] Priya: Redwood has canary rollouts per route — we can configure 10% traffic to go to quantized and monitor the evals. We'll include automatic rollback on regression threshold.
[07:00] Marcus: Good. A different question — how are we measuring cached response correctness? We want to ensure that cache hits aren't returning stale or user-specific content.
[07:08] Priya: We do conservative validation: for any cached response that contains variables we mark them as parameterized and reconstruct at serve-time; otherwise we only cache deterministic responses. We also have staleness TTLs and patch tests that run on synthetic replay to validate correctness.
[07:25] Liam: For audit, we need to see logs that show cache key creation and who requested it, timestamps and KMS key ids. Can Redwood provide these logs to our SIEM?
[07:35] Jordan: Yes, we can stream audit logs (key events) to a customer S3 or to your SIEM connector. We'll add the exact schema to the security docs.
[07:43] Liam: Also need proof of SOC2 controls around cache storage and rotation policies.
[07:48] Jordan: We'll send SOC2 attestation and a KMS integration guide.
[07:52] Marcus: Back to results — what is the cost uplift or savings projected if we get to a 60% hit-rate?
[07:58] Priya: Rough back-of-envelope: moving from 18% to 60% could cut per-token egress compute by ~45-50% for the generation endpoints, depending on burst patterns. We'll send a detailed cost model with your traffic shape.
[08:14] Marcus: Please do.
[08:16] Tom: Any surprises from the edge caches? You saw eviction thrash earlier, are there config knobs we should tune?
[08:22] Priya: Increase pool memory for the hotspot route, use a TTL tiering strategy (short TTLs for mobile flows, longer for web), and enable a small probabilistic early eviction to avoid stampedes.
[08:34] Sofia: One last thing — prompt templates: we have several variants across product teams. Should we try to centralize templates so keys align?
[08:41] Jordan: Centralizing helps a lot. Short term we can canonicalize, but long term a shared template registry is ideal.
[08:49] Marcus: We'll look into that.
[08:51] Jordan: Ok let's recap next steps and action items. Priya, you'll deliver the heatmap and enable 1h TTL on the support flow experiment. Jordan will send caching config and KMS/security docs. Marcus will upload the 24 low-hit examples. Liam and Jordan will set a security sync next week.
[09:08] Priya: quick note — the 1h TTL is only for non-personalized responses, we'll keep checkout short TTLs.
[09:15] Marcus: Sounds good.
[09:16] Avery: On product side we'll prioritize the checkout template cleanup sprint next week.
[09:20] Jordan: Great. Any final questions?
[09:23] Sofia: No.
[09:24] Liam: No.
[09:25] Jordan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the items and the dashboard links.
[09:30] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription quality: there are a few mis-heard tokens (K-V cash vs KV cache), speaker crossover around 04:00-05:00 where Tom and Sofia overlap briefly. References: shared drive link to examples (drive.company.com/novapay/poc-caching) and security deck (link provided in chat).
